turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (CAREGIVER): Ugh, sorry we're late. Traffic on the beltway was stopped dead, err, a fender bender by the exit, and then every light was red.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): I told her to turn the car around. This is nothing. Whole trip was a waste.
[SEG0003] person_3 (DOCTOR): You're in the chair now. What have you been feeling?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Little burning on the left side of my chest. Hardly anything.
[SEG0005] person_1 (CAREGIVER): Since Tuesday. He winces when he reaches up. I hid the car keys or he'd still be on the couch.
[SEG0006] person_3 (DOCTOR): Burning on the left since Tuesday. Two days, then?
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): Two days. Well, a day and a half, no, two days. Not a big deal.
[SEG0008] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any blisters, or just the burning?
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): Couple little spots. Tiny. You'd miss them.
[SEG0010] person_1 (CAREGIVER): There's a cluster on the left ribs, kind of under the arm. I saw them this morning when he got his shirt on.
[SEG0011] person_3 (DOCTOR): One side only?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah. The left. Other side's fine.
[SEG0013] person_3 (DOCTOR): Does it itch?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose. Sometimes, not really.
[SEG0015] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'll leave the itch as unclear. Any fever, chills, or feeling wiped out?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): A tiny bit warm last night. I'm not wiped out. I walked out to the mailbox.
[SEG0017] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any shortness of breath, or pain into the jaw or down the arm?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): No. None of that. It's not my heart.
[SEG0019] person_3 (DOCTOR): Cough? Pain with a deep breath?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Nope. Breathing's easy.
[SEG0021] person_3 (DOCTOR): These are the nurse's numbers. Blood pressure one oh nine over seventy-seven. Temperature thirty-eight point three.
[SEG0022] person_1 (CAREGIVER): Out in the hall she said his pulse was ninety-six. That sounded high to me.

[SEG0023] person_3 (DOCTOR): She corrected that reading. Pulse is eighty-four, not ninety-six. Separate from today, last time in March you were sixty-eight kilograms, and your last pressure was one-forty. I am not using those.
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Old numbers. I'm fine. Can we be done.
[SEG0025] person_3 (DOCTOR): Almost. Did you have chickenpox as a child?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Sure did. I was seven, uh, maybe eight. Everybody on the street had it. Ancient history.
[SEG0027] person_3 (DOCTOR): Which medicines do you take?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Amlodipine, five milligrams, for the pressure, every morning. The cholesterol one at night. Sugar tablets with breakfast. That's the real list.
[SEG0029] person_1 (CAREGIVER): And the powder. He takes Ayurvedic powder every single morning, mixed in warm water, from the shop on Hill Street.
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, only the Ayurvedic powder in the morning. A spoon. Not a real medicine, just herbs. My cousin got me on it.
[SEG0031] person_3 (DOCTOR): The cholesterol pill, what's it called, and what strength?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't remember the name. Beige little thing. It's the cholesterol one. No idea the milligrams. At night, when I remember.
[SEG0033] person_1 (CAREGIVER): He skips some nights. I keep finding them in the pill box, Monday and Thursday.
[SEG0034] person_3 (DOCTOR): And the sugar tablets, the name on the bottle?
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): Sugar tablets. White ones. Met, umm, something, I always forget. One in the morning with breakfast.

[SEG0036] person_3 (DOCTOR): Let me say it back. Amlodipine five milligrams every morning for the pressure. A cholesterol pill at night you can't name, dose unknown, and some nights get missed. Sugar tablets, one with breakfast, name unknown. Ayurvedic powder, a spoon every morning. That everything?
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, that's it. Bet the game is already in the late innings.

[SEG0038] person_1 (CAREGIVER): Oh, Marcus, his grandson, had little league on Saturday. Rain turned the outfield into a swamp and he still slid into second like it was the world series. The coach kept them out in that wind, and I was freezing up in the metal stands.

[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): Boy cannot throw a strike, but he cracks me up. Ballpark hot dogs after were terrible, which they should be. Weather was rotten all weekend too, cold and then that weird sun on the drive.
[SEG0040] person_3 (DOCTOR): Shirt up, I need to see the left side. Small cluster of blisters on a red base along the left ribs. It stops at the midline and does not cross.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): Told you. Tiny. Barely even a rash.

[SEG0042] person_3 (DOCTOR): Burning on one side for two days, blisters in a strip, and chickenpox as a boy. This looks like shingles, herpes zoster. That's a working impression, and no test has confirmed it.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): Shingles. Come on. That's an old-person thing and these spots are nothing.
[SEG0044] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'm treating it today anyway. Valacyclovere, one gram by mouth, three times a day, for seven days. Take the first dose today.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): Three times a day for a couple of spots. Fine, if you say so.
[SEG0046] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any allergies to medicines before I send it?
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing I'm allergic to.
[SEG0048] person_1 (CAREGIVER): His daughter Lisa is pregnant, about six months, and she was over Sunday putting groceries away. Should she stay away?
[SEG0049] person_3 (DOCTOR): Until the blisters crust over, Lisa and any other pregnant people should stay away, and babies too. Keep the rash covered, wash your hands, and don't share towels.
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): She'll be perfectly fine. I'll keep a shirt on. Everybody fusses.

[SEG0051] person_3 (DOCTOR): If the pain gets sharply worse, or the rash spreads past the midline, call sooner. Otherwise I'll see you back in a week. The script will be at the front desk, and finish all seven days even if the burning lets up.
[SEG0052] person_1 (CAREGIVER): I'll tell Lisa to stay home, and I'll stick the week on the fridge calendar.

spec.situation: Older person with burning pain on one side of the chest and a few blisters for two days; remembers chickenpox as a child; doctor prescribes antiviral today and gives infection advice about contact with a pregnant relative.

traps.happens: The nurse reads vital signs aloud in spoken words ('one oh nine over seventy-seven', 'thirty-eight point three') and also gives a PRIOR value ('last time in March you were sixty-eight', 'your last pressure was one-forty'). Someone may also correct a reading.
traps.label_rule: vital_signs hold only the CURRENT measured values, written normally (109/77, 38.3, 52 kg). The prior value is NOT a vital sign; it is recorded in the weight/BP entry's own notes only if the schema allows, otherwise omitted. Every number must be exactly as said; never invent or round a value that was not said.

traps.happens: The patient lists medicines with their purpose ('amlodipine for the pressure', 'the cholesterol one at night', 'sugar tablets') and also mentions a herbal or shop remedy in passing ('only the Ayurvedic powder in the morning'). Their chronic conditions are never asked about directly.
traps.label_rule: Each medicine is recorded with the dose and timing said for THAT medicine; the herbal remedy is a medicine too (currently_used). A condition the patient states through its medicine ('for the pressure') is a past_medical_history entry ONLY if the patient actually said the condition name or its everyday name ('the pressure' = hypertension, normalized); do not invent a duration.

features: ambiguous_answer: an answer that sounds like yes but is really 'maybe' ('mm, I suppose', 'sometimes, not really'); recorded with uncertainty or not at all, never as a firm fact.
tangent_small_talk: a long tangent or small talk (traffic, cricket, the weather, a grandchild) that holds NO clinical content; nothing from it is extracted.

bad.reason: Blisters/spots supported, but patient did not say left ribs; caregiver/doctor did.
bad.text: blisters (category=dermatological, status=present, temporality=current, body_site=left ribs, reported_by=patient, certainty=certain)

omissions.text: Rash/blisters are located in a cluster under the left arm/left ribs and are in a strip; this distribution detail was stated by the caregiver and doctor.
Itching was asked about and the response was equivocal/unclear ('sometimes, not really'); this symptom uncertainty was not recorded.
Fever is effectively present by measured temperature 38.3 C, not just 'feeling warm last night'.
History of prior chickenpox in childhood (around age 7-8) was stated and used in the assessment.
The diabetes medication was partially identified as 'Met, umm, something' (suggesting the bottle starts with 'Met-'), not just completely unknown 'sugar tablets'.
The doctor stated that the shingles diagnosis is a working impression and that no test has confirmed it.
